{{Short description|Austrian mathematician}}
{{similar names|Walter Mayer (disambiguation){{!}}Walter Mayer}}
[[File:Walther Mayer (cropped).jpg|thumb|Mayer in 1931]]
'''Walther Mayer''' (11 March 1887 – 10 September 1948) was an Austrian mathematician, born in [[Graz]], [[Austria-Hungary]].<ref name="pais"/> With [[Leopold Vietoris]] he is the namesake of the [[Mayer–Vietoris sequence]] in [[topology]].<ref name="t+o">{{citation|title=Tool and Object: A History and Philosophy of Category Theory|volume=32|series=Science Networks: Historical Studies|first=Ralph|last=Krömer|publisher=Springer|year=2007|isbn=9783764375249|page=51|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=41bHxtHxjUAC&pg=PA51|contribution=2.1.4 The Work of Walther Mayer on Chain Complexes}}.</ref> He served as an assistant to [[Albert Einstein]] and subsequently worked with him several years as a close collaborator,<ref name="pais">{{citation|title=Subtle is the Lord : The Science and the Life of Albert Einstein: The Science and the Life of Albert Einstein|first=Abraham|last=Pais|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=1982|isbn=9780191524028|pages=492–494|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KdaiZDaB7TgC&pg=PA492}}.</ref> leading to the nickname "Einstein's calculator".<ref>{{citation|title=How Einstein Created Relativity Out of Physics and Astronomy|volume=394|series=Astrophysics and Space Science Library|first=David|last=Topper|publisher=Springer|year=2012|isbn=9781461447818|page=137|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2U6qvi5TlE4C&pg=PA136}}.</ref>

==Biography==
Mayer studied at the [[ETH Zurich|Federal Institute of Technology]] in [[Zürich]] and the [[University of Paris]] before receiving his doctorate in 1912 from the [[University of Vienna]];<ref name="pais"/><ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=52965}}</ref> his thesis concerned the [[Fredholm integral equation]].<ref name="weibel">{{citation|title=Beyond Art: A Third Culture: A Comparative Study in Cultures, Art and Science in 20th Century Austria and Hungary|first=Peter|last=Weibel|publisher=Springer|year=2005|page=260|isbn=9783211245620|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xkk6U42Zl_sC&pg=PA260}}.</ref><ref>The title of his thesis was ''Anwendung der Fredholmschen Funktionalgleichung auf einige spezielle Randwertaufgaben des logarithmischen Potentials''.</ref> He served in the military between 1914 and 1919, during which he found time to complete a [[habilitation]] on [[differential geometry]].<ref name="weibel"/> Because he was Jewish, he had little opportunity for an academic career in Austria, and left the country; however, in 1926, with help from Einstein, he returned to a position at the [[University of Vienna]] as Privatdozent (lecturer).<ref>{{citation|first=Peter|last=Havas|contribution=Einstein, relativity, and gravitation research in Vienna before 1938|pages=161–206|title=The Expanding Worlds of General Relativity|volume=7|series=Einstein Studies|publisher=Birkhäuser|editor-first=Hubert|editor-last=Goenner|year=1999|isbn=9780817640606}}. See in particular [https://books.google.com/books?id=5mGZno8CvnQC&pg=PA167 p.&nbsp;167].</ref> He made a name for himself in [[topology]] with the [[Mayer–Vietoris sequence]],<ref name="t+o"/> and with an axiomatic treatment of [[Homology (mathematics)|homology]] predating the [[Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms]].<ref>{{citation|title=History of Topology|first=I. M.|last=James|author-link=Ioan James|publisher=Elsevier|year=1999|isbn=9780080534077|page=120|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7iRijkz0rrUC&pg=PA120}}.</ref> He also published a book on [[Riemannian geometry]] in 1930, the second volume of a textbook on differential geometry that had been started by [[Adalbert Duschek]] with a volume on curves and surfaces.<ref name="weibel"/>

In 1929, on the recommendation of [[Richard von Mises]], he became Albert Einstein's assistant with the explicit understanding that he work with him on [[teleparallelism|distant parallelism]], and from 1931 to 1936, he collaborated with [[Albert Einstein]] on the [[theory of relativity]].<ref name="pais"/> In 1933, after [[Adolf Hitler|Hitler's]] assumption of power, he followed Einstein to the United States and became an associate in mathematics at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]].<ref name="pais"/> He continued working on mathematics at the Institute, and died in Princeton in 1948.<ref name="pais"/>

==Selected publications==
* with Adalbert Duschek: ''Lehrbuch der Differentialgeometrie.'' 2 vols., Teubner 1930. [https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.493192/page/n1/mode/2up vol. 1] [https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.493119/page/n1/mode/2up vol. 2]
* ''Über abstrakte Topologie.'' In: ''[[Monatshefte für Mathematik]].'' vol. 36, 1929, pp. 1–42 (Mayer-Vietoris-Sequenzen)
* with [[Tracy Yerkes Thomas|T. Y. Thomas]]: ''Foundations of the theory of Lie groups.'' In: ''[[Annals of Mathematics]].'' 36, 1935, 770–822.
* [https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1935-038-02/S0002-9947-1935-1501812-8/S0002-9947-1935-1501812-8.pdf ''Die Differentialgeometrie der Untermannigfaltigkeiten des R''<sub>''n''</sub> ''konstanter Krümmung'']. [[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]] 38 no. 2, 1935: 267–309.
* with T. Y. Thomas: [http://www.numdam.org/item/CM_1938__5__198_0/ ''Fields of parallel vectors in non-analytic manifolds in the large'']. [[Compositio Mathematica]], vol. 5, 1938: pp. 198-207. 
* with [[Herbert Busemann]]: [https://community.ams.org/journals/tran/1941-049-02/S0002-9947-1941-0003475-2/S0002-9947-1941-0003475-2.pdf "On the foundations of calculus of variations]." Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 49, no. 2, 1941: 173-198
* ''A new homology theory.'' In: ''Annals of Mathematics.'' vol. 43, 1942, pp. 370–380, 594–605.
* ''The Duality Theory and the Basic Isomorphisms of Group Systems and Nets and Co-Nets of Group Systems.'' In: ''Annals of Mathematics.'' vol. 46, 1945, pp. 1–28
* ''On Products in Topology.'' In: ''Annals of Mathematics.'' vol. 46, 1945, pp. 29–57.
* [http://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/ksiazki/fm/fm35/fm35115.pdf ''Duality Theorems'']. In: ''[[Fundamenta Mathematicae]]'' 35, 1948, 188–202.
